extracted.intended_audience: high-school students, coaches, and contest organizers interested in USAMO/USAJMO rules, qualification, scoring, and awards
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for eligibility, index calculations, participant selection, test format, scoring, awards, and related procedures for the United States of America Mathematical Olympiad and USAJMO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility (citizenship/residency and invitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to be eligible to take the USAMO, a participant must be either a U.S. citizen or a legal resident of the United States or Canada. In addition, all participants, regardless of geographic location, must meet qualification indices determined by previous rounds of the AMC contests. Entry to the USAMO is by invitation only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only US citizens and permanent residents could be invited to the USAMO until 2003; other students legally residing in the US can be invited since 2004. Starting from IMO 2022, only U.S. permanent residents and citizens may join the American IMO team.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2025–2026 index calculation (AIME weighting change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with the 2025–2026 competition cycle, the weighting of the AIME in the calculation of AMC indices was revised. The AIME score, which had previously been multiplied by 10, is now multiplied by 20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the update, the AMC 12 index is calculated as AMC 12 score + 20 × (AIME score). Similarly, the AMC 10 index is determined by the AMC 10 score + 20 × (AIME score). Qualification cutoffs have been determined using indices prior to the 2026 season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical index calculation (pre-2025 standard formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection to the USAMO/USAJMO has commonly been based on an index defined as the student's AMC score + 10 * AIME score (historical standard used across many years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous yearly rules and selection notes use the formula 'USAMO index = AMC score + 10 * AIME score' or variations thereof for AMC10/AMC12-based indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AMC 12 vs AMC 10 indices for USAMO/USAJMO assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: AMC 12–based indices are used to select students for the USAMO, while AMC 10–based indices are used to select students for the USAJMO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a student took both AMC 10 and AMC 12 and qualified for both the USAMO and USAJMO, the student must take the USAMO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined participant quota and typical sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: The USAMO (and the USAJMO since 2010) is restricted to approximately 500 participants combined each year (250 prior to 2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both contests typically take around 200–300 students each, with the USAMO usually having 20–30 more students; exact numbers vary year-to-year and per season adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary selection by top indices (stage-based selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection is made by selecting the students with the top USAMO/USAJMO indices (examples: approximately the top ~260–330 AMC12-based indices for USAMO in various years; subsequent selections among AMC10-based indices for USAJMO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples show multi-stage selection: first select the top indices among AMC12 takers, then select high-index younger students, then add representatives from unrepresented states/territories. Exact counts for each stage have varied by year (see year-specific rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: State/territory representation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the student with the numerically largest index, whether AMC 10 based or AMC 12 based, from each U.S. state not already represented in either the USAMO or the USAJMO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The student will be invited to the USAMO if the numerically highest index in the state is AMC 12 based, and invited to the USAJMO if the index is AMC 10 based. This rule is applied after top-index selections to ensure geographic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floor-value method for younger students
rubrics_metrics.description: In some selection procedures, the lowest AIME score among the first selected (top group) determines a 'floor' value; a second selection is then made among students in a younger grade band (e.g., grades 7–10 or 10 and below) who received an AIME score at least as high as the floor value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are more young students above the floor than available slots, selection among them is done by using the USAMO index. Variations of this method appear in multiple yearly selection rules (2002–2008, 2006–2007, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional A/B contest adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: To adjust for variations in contest difficulty, the number of students selected from A & B contests will be proportional to the number of students who took the A & B contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is intended to account for differences in participation between A and B forms when allocating qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to AMC12-only eligibility for young talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Young students (AMC10 takers) who perform exceptionally on the AIME may be invited to the USAMO despite not taking AMC12; examples include AMC10 takers who score 11+ on the AIME (historical rule) being invited to USAMO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify 'unrecognized young talent'; the exact AIME cutoff and application have varied by year.

rubrics_metrics.name: USAMTS/AIME combined qualification path (2025–2026)
rubrics_metrics.description: As of the 2025–2026 season, the USAMTS competition accepts 15 people for the USAMO and 10 people for the USAJMO: the top combined scorers of the USAMTS and AIME who didn't qualify through the traditional AMC cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an alternative qualification route in addition to AMC/AIME index-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test format (post-2002)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2002, the USAMO has been a six-question, nine-hour mathematical proof competition spread out over two days. On each day, four and a half hours are given for three questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IMO uses the same format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale per problem (0–7) and score interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each question is graded on a scale from 0 to 7, with a score of 7 representing a proof that is mathematically sound. Thus, a perfect score is 42 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scale of 0 to 7 goes as follows: 0 - No work, or completely trivial work; 1–2 - Progress on the problem, but not completely solved; 3–4 - All steps are present, but may lack clarity (these scores are very rare); 5–6 - Complete solution with minor errors; 7 - Perfect solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards: rank-based and score-based thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: USAMO awards have been distributed by rank and score thresholds. For example (2022+): USAMO Gold Award approximately top 6%, Silver ~12%, Bronze ~18%; Honorable Mention: competitors who score 14 points or more (provided they did not receive a different award).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical award formats differ: earlier USAMO winners were the top 12 performers and honorable mentions the next ~12; USAJMO award structures also vary by year (top honors, honors, honorable mention with score thresholds).

rubrics_metrics.name: MOP selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Top USAMO and USAJMO participants are selected to the Mathematical Olympiad Program (MOP) through multiple criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2016, invited groups included IMO team members, the next ≈18 non-graduating USAMO students, the next ≈12 USAMO students in 9th or 10th grade, the top ≈12 students on the USAJMO, and some varying number of female contestants from USAMO/USAJMO; middle school students are invited on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam content subject expectations and calculus policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems cover algebra, number theory, combinatorics, and geometry; calculus, although allowed, is never required in solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists subject-by-problem for each year showing which subjects typically appear in each problem slot; distributions vary year-to-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test administration procedures (posting, collection, and venues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2002, test problems have been posted on the AMC website fifteen minutes prior to the official start of the test. Student responses are then faxed back to the AMC office at the end of the testing period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most years, students have taken the USAMO at their respective high schools. The MAA introduced official competition sites for the 2026 USA(J)MO to create a more controlled setting and reduce the risk of academic dishonesty; many sites are university institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical format variations (pre-2002 and earlier scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier formats differed: 1996–2001 consisted of two three-problem sets with three hours each; 1995 and earlier had five problems in three and a half hours (earlier, three hours) with each problem worth 20 points (perfect score 100).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These historical formats explain past scoring systems and time allocations and appear in the page for historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional/contingency procedures (COVID-19 adaptations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the AIME II and the USA(J)MO were postponed and eventually run as online competitions renamed AOIME (American Online Invitational Mathematics Examination) and USO(J)MO (United States Online (Junior) Mathematical Olympiad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2020 saw reduced qualifier counts and rescheduled online administration; such exceptional adaptations may be used when necessary.
